sweep_summary: Title sweep for Santali yielded one item only, and it is a Glottolog mislink: Corriente 1998 'On some features of late Granadian Arabic (mostly stress)' is tagged Santali by Glottolog's 'computerized assignment from \"mostly\"' (record 607548 fetched sources and saved); it concerns Andalusi Arabic and has no bearing on the catalog. No new Santali stress literature surfaced from titles. Re-read the on-disk first-hand sources: Bodding 1929 page images pp.133–134 confirm the catalog's deciding §155 quotation verbatim plus §157(c) ('Dissyllabic words may have stress on either the first or the second syllable'), so the 'undetermined' coding is page-grade; Ghosh 2008 §2.5 p.30 states fixed second-syllable stress; Horo & Anderson 2021 (JSEALS SP8, open, on file) instrumentally find second-syllable prominence in Assam Santali disyllables, quantity-insensitive, while calling the descriptive literature contradictory. Best new statement = Horo & Anderson 2021 abstract p.298; it refines but does not supersede Bodding for the general coding. Still unread: Horo & Anderson 2022 (Deccan College volume, not located; medium priority) and Neukom 2001 p.8 (Lincom grammar; only Neukom 2000 'Argument marking in Santali' is open on archive.org).

new_statements.quote: Based on subsequent instrumental analysis, we suggest that Assam Santali always shows prominence on the second syllable of disyllables, cued by intensity, f0 and duration–a pattern like that attested in Assam and Odisha lects of Sora (Horo and Sarmah 2015, Horo 2017, Horo et al. 2020), contra Donegan and Stampe (2004)–an iambic pattern and not quantity sensitive, at least in disyllables.
new_statements.citation: Horo, Luke & Gregory D. S. Anderson. 2021. Towards a prosodic typology of Kherwarian Munda languages: Santali of Assam. Papers from SEALS 30 (JSEALS Special Publication 8), 298–314.
new_statements.reading: Instrumental evidence (duration, intensity, f0; three utterance frames; male and female speakers) that in the Sonitpur (Assam) lect, uninflected disyllabic words are prominent on the second syllable regardless of syllable weight — i.e. fixed second-syllable / iambic, agreeing with Ghosh 2008:30 ('always on the second syllable') and against Neukom 2001:8 (quantity-sensitive, initial default) and Bodding 1929 §155/§157(c) (lexically fixed, either syllable). It is preliminary, limited to disyllables and to one previously undescribed variety, so it does not by itself settle placement for Santali as a whole; the catalog's 'undetermined' coding, grounded in Bodding's page-verified §155, still stands, but the modern sources (Ghosh 2008 + this study) converge on second-syllable stress and are the recode candidate if the catalog later prefers modern descriptions over Bodding.

sources.quote: Based on subsequent instrumental analysis, we suggest that Assam Santali always shows prominence on the second syllable of disyllables, cued by intensity, f0 and duration–a pattern like that attested in Assam and Odisha lects of Sora (Horo and Sarmah 2015, Horo 2017, Horo et al. 2020), contra Donegan and Stampe (2004)–an iambic pattern and not quantity sensitive, at least in disyllables.
sources.note: Only instrumental study: for one lect (Sonitpur district, Assam), uninflected disyllables carry second-syllable prominence (duration robust; intensity less so; f0 higher on syllable 2 only in phrasal/unaccented frames, not in isolation). Authors call the prior literature 'a chaotic picture of contradictory analyses' (Ghosh 2008:30 fixed 2nd; Neukom 2001:8 QS with initial default; Bodding 1922 partly morpholexical). Refines but does not settle the general coding; preliminary, disyllables only, one variety.

sources.citation: Ghosh, Arun. 2008. Santali. In G. D. S. Anderson (ed.), The Munda Languages (Routledge Language Family Series), 11–98. London: Routledge.
sources.quote: Stress is always on the second syllable of a word unless it is monosyllabic, irrespective of whether it is an open or a closed syllable. [p.30] ... In words with more than one syllable the second syllable gets the stress. [p.31] ... Words are predominantly dissyllabic with stress on the second syllable in dissyllabic and multisyllabic words, and on the root vowel if it is monosyllabic. [p.11]
sources.note: Fixed second-syllable stress (quantity-insensitive), stated three times without examples of stressed forms. Contradicts Bodding's lexical/either-syllable description; the catalog record already notes this as the only live recode reading (fixed 2nd) and blocks it at page grade on Bodding and Neukom.

sources.quote: 155. There is in the language no fixed general rule for where stress is to be applied, whether on the first or on the last syllable of a word (or unit) or elsewhere. The stress may be anywhere, only that in the same word it will remain in the same place, except as noted below. [...] (c) Dissyllabic words may have stress on either the first or the second syllable. Certain rules followed by the language in regard to such words are discernible. (d) Dissyllabic words formed by reduplication of a monosyllabic base [...] have a slightly perceptible preponderance of stress on ultima [...] ba'ba (father), [...] but 'gongo
sources.note: Page images re-read: the catalog's deciding quotation is verbatim on p.133; p.134 §157(c) states disyllables may stress either syllable, with partly morpholexical sub-rules (reduplicated/infixed disyllables ultima-stressed). Confirms the catalog's 'undetermined' coding.
